interactions.label: A dendritic cell presents an antigen on MHC class II to a CD4-positive T helper

params.question: A dendritic cell presents an antigen on MHC class II to a CD4-positive T helper cell, which differentiates into the Th1 subset. Which downstream immune response does this Th1 cell activate?

answers.text: Antibody class switching via interleukin-4 and eosinophil recruitment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes the Th2 response. Th2 cells secrete interleukin-4, driving B cell class switching and recruiting eosinophils — important in allergic responses and helminth defence.

answers.text: Macrophage activation through interferon-gamma to kill intracellular pathogens

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Th1 cells produce interferon-gamma and tumour necrosis factor, which activate macrophages to destroy intracellular pathogens such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

answers.text: Neutrophil recruitment through interleukin-17 against extracellular fungi

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes the Th17 response. Th17 cells produce interleukin-17, recruiting neutrophils primarily to combat extracellular bacteria and fungi.

answers.text: Immune suppression through interleukin-10 and transforming growth factor beta

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes the function of regulatory T cells (Tregs), not Th1 cells. Tregs suppress excessive immune responses to maintain self-tolerance.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the four CD4 subsets: Th1 activates macrophages (IFN-γ), Th2 drives antibody switching (IL-4), Th17 recruits neutrophils (IL-17), and Tregs suppress responses (IL-10, TGF-β).
Correct! Th1 cells are the macrophage-activating subset, using interferon-gamma to enhance intracellular killing.

interactions.label: Both Goodpasture syndrome and lupus nephritis cause renal damage through antibod

params.question: Both Goodpasture syndrome and lupus nephritis cause renal damage through antibody-mediated mechanisms. Which statement correctly explains why serum complement levels differ between these two conditions?

answers.text: In Goodpasture (Type II), complement activation is localised to the basement membrane, so serum levels remain normal; in lupus nephritis (Type III), circulating immune complexes consume complement systemically

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Type II reactions target fixed tissue antigens, keeping complement consumption localised. Type III reactions involve circulating immune complexes that consume complement systemically, causing measurably low C3 and C4 during active flares.

answers.text: Goodpasture does not involve complement activation at all, whereas lupus nephritis activates it through the alternative pathway

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Goodpasture syndrome does activate complement — this contributes to tissue damage — but the activation is confined to the glomerular basement membrane and does not deplete circulating levels.

answers.text: Complement levels are low in both conditions because both activate the classical pathway via antigen-antibody complexes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While both involve antibodies and can activate complement, the critical distinction is localised versus systemic consumption. Only Type III reactions consume enough complement to measurably reduce serum levels.

answers.text: Both conditions activate complement equally, but the kidney excretes complement faster in lupus nephritis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Complement is not excreted by the kidney. The difference lies in whether complement consumption is localised to the tissue (Type II) or occurs systemically through circulating immune complexes (Type III).

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: in Goodpasture (Type II), antibodies bind the basement membrane directly and complement activation stays localised. In SLE nephritis (Type III), circulating immune complexes consume complement systemically, dropping C3 and C4.
Correct! Localised versus systemic complement consumption is the key distinction between Type II and Type III hypersensitivity.

interactions.label: C4d deposition in a transplanted kidney is the Banff marker of acute cellular re

params.question: C4d deposition in a transplanted kidney is the Banff marker of acute cellular rejection driven by recipient T lymphocytes.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: C4d marks antibody-mediated (humoral) rejection, not cellular rejection. The video distinguishes the two forms: cellular rejection involves T lymphocyte infiltration, whereas antibody-mediated rejection deposits C4d through complement activation by donor-specific antibodies.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: C4d is the Banff footprint of antibody-mediated (humoral) rejection, not cellular rejection. It indicates complement activation by donor-specific antibodies. Cellular rejection is diagnosed by T lymphocyte infiltration on biopsy — a fundamentally different mechanism.

interactions.label: A patient with systemic lupus erythematosus has rising anti-double-stranded DNA

params.question: A patient with systemic lupus erythematosus has rising anti-double-stranded DNA titres and falling serum C3 and C4 levels. Which pathological sequence best explains this combination?

answers.text: Falling complement causes autoantibody production through loss of immune regulation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The causation runs the other way. Complement deficiency (e.g., C1q) can predispose to SLE, but during an active flare, falling complement is a consequence of immune complex consumption, not a cause of autoantibody production.

answers.text: Anti-dsDNA antibodies activate the alternative complement pathway, consuming C3 but sparing C4

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: SLE immune complexes activate complement through the classical pathway (C1q binding to antigen-antibody complexes), which consumes both C3 and C4. The alternative pathway primarily consumes C3 and factor B.

answers.text: Anti-dsDNA antibodies directly bind and inactivate circulating C3 and C4 without forming immune complexes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Anti-dsDNA antibodies do not directly bind or inactivate complement proteins. The mechanism requires immune complex formation: antibodies bind nuclear antigens, complexes deposit in tissues, and the resulting classical pathway activation consumes complement.

answers.text: Anti-dsDNA antibodies form immune complexes that deposit in tissues, consuming complement via the classical pathway

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Anti-dsDNA antibodies bind nuclear antigens to form circulating immune complexes. These deposit in glomeruli, vessels, and serosal surfaces, activating the classical complement pathway and consuming both C3 and C4. Rising anti-dsDNA with falling complement signals an active flare.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review SLE pathogenesis: anti-dsDNA antibodies form immune complexes → deposit in tissues → activate classical complement → consume C3 and C4. Rising antibody titres with falling complement marks an active flare.
Correct! Immune complex formation and classical pathway complement consumption is the central pathological mechanism in active SLE.

interactions.label: A patient tests negative on a fourth-generation ELISA ten days after high-risk H

params.question: A patient tests negative on a fourth-generation ELISA ten days after high-risk HIV exposure, yet HIV RNA by PCR returns positive. Which concept best explains this discrepancy?

answers.text: Fourth-generation ELISA detects only antibodies, not antigens, so it misses early infection entirely

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Fourth-generation ELISA detects both p24 antigen and antibodies simultaneously, which is why it turns positive earlier than antibody-only tests. However, even this combined detection has a window period of approximately two weeks.

answers.text: HIV RNA PCR frequently produces false-positive results in the first month after exposure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: HIV RNA PCR is a highly specific test used precisely to diagnose infection during the window period. False positivity is not a significant concern in this clinical context.

answers.text: The ELISA was performed during the window period, when p24 antigen and antibodies are below detection thresholds but viral RNA is already present

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: During the window period (approximately the first two weeks), HIV is replicating and RNA is detectable by PCR within days, but p24 antigen and antibodies have not yet reached the ELISA detection threshold. RNA testing bridges this diagnostic gap.

answers.text: The patient carries the CCR5-delta-32 homozygous mutation, which blocks ELISA detection but not RNA amplification

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CCR5-delta-32 homozygosity confers resistance to HIV infection by preventing viral entry via the CCR5 co-receptor. It does not affect ELISA detection. A negative ELISA at day ten is explained by the window period, not a genetic variant.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the HIV diagnostic algorithm: fourth-generation ELISA detects p24 antigen and antibodies (positive at ~2 weeks). During the window period, HIV RNA PCR can detect the virus within days of infection.
Correct! The window period explains why an early ELISA may be negative despite active HIV infection — RNA testing bridges this diagnostic gap.
